title: Ways to Run Linux
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Ways to Run Linux and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate ways to run linux.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces ways to run linux as part of linux installation and environment setup. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Choose and prepare an appropriate practice environment while protecting existing data and verifying installation media.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks.

items.title: Installing on physical hardware
items.text: Installing on physical hardware: Use the tool appropriate to the distribution, inspect proposed changes first, and note the package/runtime version that determines behavior.

items.text: Virtual machines: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.text: Cloud-based Linux virtual machines: Try a small reproducible command with quoted inputs, inspect standard output and error separately, and check the exit status as well as the printed text.

items.text: Containers versus full operating systems: Start with a baseline, correlate the observation with the process or workload, and avoid inferring a bottleneck from a single metric.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Ways to Run Linux. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume ways to run linux behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: The sample data is synthetic and the pipeline does not read private logs. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate ways to run linux. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks.
Use evidence rather than assumptions; make platform differences explicit.
Protect credentials and data, and plan how to reverse state-changing operations.
